Kaggle Plant Disease Classification

hbmaclean

2025-08-04

1 Introduction

This is just another side project to keep me learning. I picked this one in particular to try a source other than UCI and because it had some notebooks listed that I can gauge against. I scanned about five of the notebooks - all were python-based, looked very similar, and had accuracy around 75-85%.

Below is a description of the data from Kaggle.

Plant diseases cause significant agricultural losses worldwide. Early prediction of disease outbreaks can help farmers take preventive measures. This synthetic dataset simulates environmental conditions that might lead to fungal infections in plants.

The dataset contains 10,000 samples representing environmental measurements from different farm locations with the following features: 

  • temperature: Measured in degrees Celsius 

  • humidity: Measured as percentage 

  • rainfall: Measured in millimeters 

  • soil_pH: Acidity/alkalinity measurement 

  • disease_present: Binary label (0 = healthy, 1 = diseased)

2 Importing Packages

repo <- "http://cran.us.r-project.org"
packages <- c(
    'curl', 'stringr', 'dplyr', 'tidyr', 'data.table', 'caret', 'tibble',
    'kableExtra', 'ggcorrplot', 'gridExtra', 'GGally', 'stats', 'rstatix',
    'ranger', 'tuneRanger', 'mlr', 'randomForest', 'missMethods', 'nnet',
    'naivebayes', 'matrixStats', 'earth', 'mda', 'hda', 'bnclassify', 'rocc',
    'VGAM', 'HiDimDA', 'DT', 'devtools'
)
for (package in packages) {
    if (!require(package, character.only = TRUE)) {
        install.packages(package, repos = repo)
        library(package, character.only = TRUE)
    }
}

install_github('munoztd0/reprtree')
eval(substitute(library(pkg), list(pkg='reprtree')))
library(reprtree)

set.seed(34)

3 Fetching the Data

Rather than setting up API keys and assuming the reader will do the same, I fetch instead with curl. Straightforward, other than that the CSV has column names in the first row.

fetch_data <- function() {
    options(timeout = 120)
    url <- paste0(
        'https://www.kaggle.com/api/v1/datasets/download/',
        'turakut/plant-disease-classification'
    )
    tmp <- tempfile()
    curl_download(url, tmp)
    data <- as.data.frame(
        read.csv(
            unz(tmp, 'plant_disease_dataset.csv'),
            header = FALSE,   # first row has column names
            skip = 1          # skip them
        )
    )
    colnames(data) <- c(
        'temperature', 'humidity', 'rainfall', 'soil_ph', 'disease_present'
    )
    return(data)
}

ggpairs(plant_df)

6.4 Analysis of Variance (AOV)

AOV does caution that it works best with balanced designs - and I assume this is NOT, given the class distribution of about 75%/25%. Otherwise, I would conclude that rainfall and humidity are most influential.

unclass(summary(stats::aov(disease_present ~ ., data = plant_df))) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column(var = 'Column') |>
    filter(!is.na(F.value)) |>
    mutate(Column = reorder(Column, desc(F.value))) |>
    ggplot(aes(Mean.Sq, F.value, color = Column)) +
    geom_point(cex = 4) +
    scale_x_log10()

Concluding this topic, there is no apparent room for reduction. corr, pca, and nzv will surely not be worthwhile preProcess options.

7 Initial Model Framework

Here I create functions for making predictions, calculating accuracy, running individual models, tracking results, and easily running them all together. The goal is to run numerous models and then narrow down to the most accurate one or few.

7.1 Predictions and Accuracy

Below are functions to make predictions and calculate accuracy, using the ellipsis argument to allow model nuances to be passed in.

predictions <- function(model, test_df, ...) {
    pred <- predict(model, test_df, ...)
    if (is.atomic(pred)) {
        predictions <- pred
    }
    else {
        predictions <- pred$predictions
    }
    predictions
}

accuracy <- function(model, test_df, verbose = FALSE, ...) {
    acc <- NA
    tryCatch({
        pred <- predictions(model, test_df, ...)
        cm   <- confusionMatrix(pred, factor(test_df$disease_present))
        acc  <- round(100*cm$overall[['Accuracy']], 3)
    },
    error = function(e) {
        if (verbose) {
            sprintf('model %s, error %s', class(model), e)
        }
    },
    finally = {
        return(acc)
    })
}

7.2 Formula and Models

And here, a basic formula; and a function for each model.

fc <- as.formula(factor(disease_present) ~ .)

ranger__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc) {
    fit <- ranger(formula, train_df)
    accuracy(fit, test_df)
}

rf__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc) {
    fit <- randomForest(formula, train_df, ntree = 20)
    accuracy(fit, test_df)
}

multinom__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc) {
    fit <- multinom(formula, train_df, trace = FALSE, decay = .00015)
    accuracy(fit, test_df)
}

naive_bayes__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc) {
    fit <- naive_bayes(formula, train_df, usekernel = TRUE)
    accuracy(fit, test_df)
}

avNNet__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc) {
    fit <- avNNet(formula, train_df, size = 5, trace = FALSE)
    accuracy(fit, test_df, type = 'class')
}

knn3__c <- function(train_df, test_df, formula = fc, ...) {
    fit <- knn3(formula, train_df, ...)
    accuracy(fit, test_df, type = 'class')
}

7.3 Model Runner

Finally, a function to actually run the models and accumulate metrics.

run_models <- function(.train = train_df, .test = test_df, ...) {
    results <- vector()
    results <- append(results, c(
        ranger__c(.train, .test, ...),
        rf__c(.train, .test, ...),
        multinom__c(.train, .test, ...),
        naive_bayes__c(.train, .test, ...),
        avNNet__c(.train, .test, ...),
        knn3__c(.train, .test, k = 13)
    ))
    names(results) <- c('ranger', 'rf', 'multinom', 'naive_bayes', 'avNNet', 'knn3')
    return(results)
}

7.4 Metrics Summary

Below, a function to display the metrics. At the moment, the expectation is that the named vector from run_models will be bound with an initial column of meaningful labels.

display_summary <- function(.data) {
    .data |>
        dplyr::rename(` ` = c(1)) |>
        datatable(
            rownames = FALSE,
            width    = '75%',
            options  = list(
                dom        = 't',
                pageLength = nrow(.data)
            )
        )
}

7.5 Initial Runs - Baseline, Imputing, Scaling, Centering

With the framework defined, I run the models in various scenarios - imputing outliers, scaling, and centering.

model_summary <- bind_rows(
    run_models(),
    run_models(.train = impute_mean(train_o)),
    run_models(.train = impute_median(train_o)),
    run_models(
        .train = train_df |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=FALSE, scale=TRUE))),
        .test  = test_df  |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=FALSE, scale=TRUE)))
    ),
    run_models(
        .train = train_df |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=TRUE, scale=FALSE))),
        .test  = test_df  |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=TRUE, scale=FALSE)))
    ),
    run_models(
        .train = train_df |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=TRUE, scale=TRUE))),
        .test  = test_df  |>
            mutate(across(-c(disease_present), ~ scale(.x, center=TRUE, scale=TRUE)))
    )
)
model_summary <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'baseline', 'mean-impute outliers', 'median-impute outliers',
        'scaled', 'centered', 'centered & scaled'
    ),
    model_summary
)

display_summary(model_summary)

8 Second Model Framework - train()

From above, ranger and randomForest look best - always above 80%. Here, I look more closely at those two using train, hoping to tune them better with preProcess, tuneGrid, and trainControl.

8.1 Models and Tuning

Many models seem to be available only via train; others are available directly but do not conform to the typical fit/predict/confusionMatrix pattern. Since I am building a framework to run ranger and randomForest via train, I also chose additional classification models that I have used before or sampled arbitrarily now from this caret list.

First, I define a list of tuneGrid objects for the models, each NULL by default; with the names serving as a proxy for the list of models.

tuning  <- list(
    'ranger'        = NULL,
    'rf'            = NULL,
    'Rborist'       = NULL,
    'svmRadial'     = NULL,
    'mlp'           = NULL,
    'xgbTree'       = NULL,
    'gamLoess'      = NULL,
    'rocc'          = NULL,
   #'hda'           = NULL,   <---- omitted, hopelessly verbose
    'glmnet'        = NULL,
    'treebag'       = NULL,
    'vglmContRatio' = NULL,
    'RFlda'         = NULL,
    'lssvmRadial'   = NULL
)

This is admittedly a shotgun approach, but it exposes me to more models. I actually chose more models, but skipped any that failed for any reason. Some require packages that are not in the usual location; and the following failed with, “all the Accuracy metric values are missing”:

  • gbm, fda, awnb, bagFDAGCV, ada, rpartCost, dwdRadial, randomGLM, binda, lssvmLinear

I have encountered the error before and I suspect that either it could be resolved with appropriate tuning, or the model is simply not designed for the data. I may try to solve that some other day.

8.2 Running the Models via Train

Here I write a function to generically execute a model via train and capture its accuracy. Arguments allow for alternate data sets, formula, model list, trControl and lists of tuneGrid objects; and the ellipsis argument implicitly allows for preProcess and whatever else might be applicable.

execute_models <- function(
    .train        = train_df,
    .test         = test_df,
    .formula      = fc,
    .models       = names(tuning),
    .tuning       = tuning[c(.models)],
    .trControl    = trainControl(method = 'repeatedcv', number = 2, p = .5),
    .preProcess   = c('center', 'scale'),
    bestTune      = FALSE,
    verbose       = FALSE,
    ...
) {
    results <- vector()
    results <- mapply(
        function(model, tune, ...) {
            acc <- NA
            tryCatch({
                fit <- caret::train(
                      .formula,
                      method        = model,
                      data          = .train,
                      trControl     = .trControl,
                      tuneGrid      = tune,
                      preProcess    = .preProcess,
                      trace         = FALSE,
                      verbosity     = 0,
                      verbose       = FALSE,
                      na.action     = na.pass,
                      ...
                )
                acc <- accuracy(fit, .test)
            },
            error = function(e) {
                if (verbose) {
                    print(c(Model = model, error = e))
                }
            },
            finally = {
                results <- append(results, acc)
                if (bestTune && !is.null(acc)) {
                    print(c(Model = model, bestTune = fit$bestTune))
                }
            })
        },
        .models,
        .tuning,
        ...
    )
    if (is.vector(results) & length(names(results))>1) {
        return(bind_rows(results))
    }
    else {
        return(results)
    }
}

8.4 Tuning the Top Five Models

Next I’ll focus on the top five models, which appropriately are all forestry-related in name. First I will dig into each model’s tundGrid.

It proved to be a little tricky passing in the tuneGrid for a single model. Since I’ve implemented .tuning as an argument to mapply, a list is expected. Passing in a single tuneGrid gives an error, “incorrect number of dimensions”.

Below is one example; and for xbgTree I had to be careful to NOT create too large a grid!

execute_models(
    .models = c('xgbTree'),
    .tuning = list(expand.grid(
        nrounds          = 10,
        max_depth        = c(2:5),
        eta              = c(.5,.7,.9),
        gamma            = c(3:6),
        colsample_bytree = c(.7,.8,.9),
        min_child_weight = c(5,10,15),
        subsample        = 1
    )),
    bestTune = TRUE
)

Below are the settings I settled on. Fiddling them further did not change accuracy much in either direction.

tuning <- list(
    xgbTree    = expand.grid(
        nrounds          = 50,
        max_depth        = 3,
        eta              = .1,
        gamma            = .9,
        colsample_bytree = seq(.8,1,.1),
        min_child_weight = c(1:3),
        subsample        = c(1:2)
    ),
    ranger     = data.frame(
        mtry          = 2,
        splitrule     = 'hellinger',
        min.node.size = 50
    ), 
    rf      = data.frame(mtry = 2),
    Rborist = data.frame(predFixed = 2, minNode   = 2),
    treebag = NULL
)
tuned <- execute_models()
tuned |>
    pivot_longer(everything()) |>
    arrange(desc(value)) |>
    kable(col.names = c('Model', 'Accuracy')) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = 'left')
Model Accuracy

rf 86.10
Rborist 86.08

8.5 Pre-Processing the Top Five Models

With the top five models tuned, I look into other preProcess methods.

Note, “all the Accuracy metric values are missing” occurs again with the following methods:

  • ‘conditionalX’
  • ‘knnImpute’
  • ‘BoxCox’, but only when adjusting the associated ‘fudge’ parameter, and then only for ‘ranger’ and ‘rf’
preprocessed <- bind_rows(
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('BoxCox')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('YeoJohnson')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('expoTrans')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('center')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('scale')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('center', 'scale')),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('bagImpute'), .train = train_o),
    execute_models(.preProcess = c('medianImpute'), .train = train_o)
)

And the results:

model_summary <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'baseline', 'tuned',
        'BoxCox', 'YeoJohnson', 'expoTrans', 'center', 'scale',
        'center+scale', 'bagImpute', 'medianImpute'
    ),
    bind_rows(baselines[c(names(tuned))], tuned, preprocessed),
)

display_summary(model_summary)

Conclusions from this:

  • as seen earlier projects, imputing outliers has a measurably harmful effect
  • otherwise, various preProcess options made minor improvements over the ‘tuned’ models
  • treebag is lagging - its best accuracy is less than the others’ least, other than imputing

8.6 trainControl Methods for the Top Five Models

Now I try various trainControl methods. For simplicity, I rely mostly on underlying default values; and specify only method, and constant number = 2 rather than default 10 or 25, for performance reasons.

# Note, there is also LOOCV (leave-one-out CV) but it is computationally *intense*
trcontrolled <- bind_rows(
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'boot')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'boot632')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'boot_all')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'optimism_boot')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(method = 'adaptive_boot')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'cv')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'repeatedcv')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(method = 'adaptive_cv')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(number = 2, method = 'LGOCV')),
    execute_models(.trControl = trainControl(method = 'adaptive_LGOCV'))
)
trcontrolled <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'boot', 'boot632', 'boot_all', 'optimism_boot', 'adaptive_boot',
        'cv', 'repeatedcv', 'adaptive_cv', 'LGOCV', 'adaptive_LGOCV'
    ),
    trcontrolled
)

model_summary <- bind_rows(model_summary, trcontrolled)
display_summary(model_summary)

8.7 Formula Modifications

I understand the syntax of what I’m doing here, but I cannot envision the underlying mechanics. I have no expectations, just another experiment.

formulamods <- bind_rows(
    execute_models(
        .formula = as.formula(factor(disease_present) ~ humidity*rainfall + .)
    ),
    execute_models(
        .formula = as.formula(
            factor(disease_present) ~ humidity:rainfall + .
        )
    ),
    execute_models(
        .formula = as.formula(
            factor(disease_present) ~ (humidity+rainfall+temperature)^3 + .
        )
    ),
    execute_models(
        .formula = as.formula(
            factor(disease_present) ~ (humidity+rainfall+temperature)^3 + I(soil_ph^2)
        )
    )
)

formulamods <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'humidity*rain', 'humidity:rain', '(humidity+rain+temp)^3',
        '(humidity+rain+temp)^3 + ph^2'
    ),
    formulamods
)

model_summary <- bind_rows(model_summary, formulamods)
display_summary(model_summary)

That had a negative effect, though not quite as bad as imputing.

Note, I tried similar formulas when running the models directly (without train) but continually failed with, “One or more independent variables not found in data.”

9 Final Efforts with Top Two

9.1 Combinations of Isolated Improvements

Looking at the running summary, some settings appeared to make minor improvements beyond the initial tuning, in isolation. I certainly do not assume that combining such improvements will result in a combined improvement - but I will try some combinations, for the top two models.

The following settings showed some promise for xgbTree and ranger, all somewhat above baseline accuracy. The table is not meant to convey combinations; the two columns are independent, each setting was in isolation.

10 Loose Ends

10.1 Ranger Case- and Class Weights

ranger supports case- and class weights. I have used them before and know they can be very effective at balancing lopsided data. So far I’ve found the balancing to be a zero-sum effort in terms of accuracy/RMSE; for example, accuracy for true negatives may improve at the expense of true positives.

I create case weights (weighing each observation) with parsnip::importance_weights and, just a guess, rowSds.

To weigh the two classes, I refer again to this article.

.case_weights = parsnip::importance_weights(
    rowSds(train_df[1:4] |> as.matrix()) |>
    as.vector()
)
.class_weights <- c(
    nrow(train_df) / (2 * sum(train_df$disease_present == 0)),
    nrow(train_df) / (2 * sum(train_df$disease_present == 1))
)

I know from the past that weights may work seamlessly via train for bootstrap methods; but fail for cross-validation methods. This makes sense, as each cross-validation fold will be shorter in length than the full list of weights. I use a known workaround for cv, after trying train and bootstrap.

10.1.1 Weights with Bootstrap via Train

.boot <- bind_rows(
      execute_models(
          .models        = c('ranger'),
          .trControl     = trainControl(method = 'boot'),
          .preProcess    = c('center')
      ),
      execute_models(
          .models        = c('ranger'),
          .trControl     = trainControl(method = 'boot'),
          .preProcess    = c('center'),
          case.weights   = list(.case_weights)
      ),
      execute_models(
          .models        = c('ranger'),
          .trControl     = trainControl(method = 'boot'),
          .preProcess    = c('center'),
          class.weights  = list(.class_weights)
      ),
      execute_models(
          .models        = c('ranger'),
          .trControl     = trainControl(method = 'boot'),
          .preProcess    = c('center'),
          case.weights   = list(.case_weights),
          class.weights  = list(.class_weights)
      )
)

10.1.2 Weights with Cross-Validation

Here I simulate cross-validation per this solution, iterating over 10 folds. It begs the question though, given one accuracy result per fold, what is the final accuracy? Perhaps average?

n            <- nrow(train_df)
num_folds    <- 10
folds        <- split(sample(n), cut(1:n, num_folds, labels = FALSE))

.cv <- sapply(folds, function(fold) {
    .test  <- train_df[fold,]
    .train <- train_df[-fold,]
    fit    <- ranger(factor(disease_present) ~ ., .train)
    fit_a  <- ranger(factor(disease_present) ~ ., .train, case.weights = .case_weights[-fold])
    fit_b  <- ranger(factor(disease_present) ~ ., .train, class.weights = .class_weights)
    fit_ab <- ranger(factor(disease_present) ~ ., .train, case.weights = .case_weights[-fold], class.weights = .class_weights)
    c(
        baseline     = accuracy(fit, .test),
        caseWeights  = accuracy(fit_a, .test),
        classWeights = accuracy(fit_b, .test),
        bothWeights  = accuracy(fit_ab, .test)
    )
})

And the results:

bind_cols(
    c('baseline', 'caseWeights', 'classWeights', 'bothWeights'),
    .cv,
    .boot
) |> kable(col.names = c('', paste(rep('fold',10), 1:10), '')) |>
     add_header_above(c('', 'cross-validation' = 10, 'boot' = 1)) |>
     kable_styling(

I leave open the question whether weights helped balance specificity and sensitivity.

10.1.3 Weights with dplyr

This article suggests another approach, which I will try here.

execute_models(
    .models        = c('ranger'),
    .trControl     = trainControl(method = 'cv'),
    .preProcess    = c('center'),
    .train         = train_df |> dplyr::mutate(
        case_wts = parsnip::importance_weights(.class_weights[disease_present+1])
    ),
    .test          = test_df  |> dplyr::mutate(
        case_wts = parsnip::importance_weights(.class_weights[disease_present+1])
    )
)
## ranger 
##    100

Hold on, this must be cheating - it creates another binary column having 100% correlation with the outcome…

This seems equivalent to setting case_wts = disease_present, or adding the outcome to the right hand side of the formula, e.g. factor(disease_present) ~ . + disease_present (both of which also give 100% accuracy.)

10.2 Custom-Tuning Ranger

While poking around, I found tuneRanger. Its tuneMtryFast indicates that the out-of-bag (OOB) error varies very little for any mtry near 1. (I did not know that mtry could be zero or fractional.)

sink(nullfile())
res <- tuneMtryFast(
    fc,
    data       = train_df,
    mtryStart  = .1,
    stepFactor = .1,
    improve    = .05,
    trace      = FALSE,
    plot       = FALSE
)
sink()
plot(res, type = 'b')

10.2.1 Comparing tuneRanger/ranger and Positive Class

The package also provides some other tools worth trying. Here I try tuneRanger, which first needs a “task” object from mlr. Then, evidently, estimateTimeTuneRanger will estimate how long to expect to process the “task” with tuneRanger; and a prediction can be made with the result of tuneRanger.

Out of curiosity I also fit ranger directly with the recommended tuning from tuneRanger to compare their accuracy.

While preparing this, I notice makeCLassifTask has a positive parameter to indicate the positive class, so I put this in a repeatable function and collect the metrics for both classes.

compare_tuneRanger_and_ranger <- function(positive_class) {
    # 1. Create classification task
    task <- mlr::makeClassifTask(
        data     = train_df,
        target   = 'disease_present',
        positive = positive_class 
    )
    
    # 2. Get its estimated execution time (suppressing other output)
    sink(nullfile())
    etime <- estimateTimeTuneRanger(task)
    sink()
    
    # 3. Execute task, capturing time
    rtime <- system.time(
        res <- tuneRanger(
            task,
            measure        = list(acc), # or multiclass.brier,, auc, logloss, ...
            num.trees      = 1000,
            num.threads    = 2,
            iters          = 20,
            save.file.path = NULL,
            show.info      = FALSE
        )
    )

    # 4. Predict with tuneRanger model
    pred      <- predict(res$model, newdata = test_df)
    
    # 5. Calculate its accuracy
    tuned_acc <- pred$data |>
        as.data.frame() |>
        dplyr::summarize(acc = 100*sum(truth == response)/n()) |>
        pull(acc)
    
    # 6. Fit ranger with the recommended parameter settings
    fit <- ranger(
        fc,
        train_df,
        mtry            = res$recommended.pars$mtry,
        min.node.size   = res$recommended.pars$min.node.size,
        sample.fraction = res$recommended.pars$sample.fraction
    )

    # 7. Report it
    tribble(
        ~PositiveClass, ~Estimated, ~Actual,
        ~Estimated, ~tuneRanger, ~ranger,
        ~mtry, ~min.node.size, ~sample.fraction,
        positive_class, etime, rtime['elapsed'],
        100*res$recommended.pars$acc,
        tuned_acc,
        accuracy(fit, test_df),
        res$recommended.pars$mtry,
        res$recommended.pars$min.node.size,
        round(res$recommended.pars$sample.fraction, 4)
    )
}

# 8. Blend the results
class1 <- compare_tuneRanger_and_ranger(positive_class = 1)
class0 <- compare_tuneRanger_and_ranger(positive_class = 0)
rbind(class1, class0) |>
    kable(digits = 3) |>
    add_header_above(
        c(' ' = 1, 'Time' = 2, 'Accuracy' = 3, 'Recommendations' = 3),
        underline = TRUE
    ) |> 
    kable_paper()
Time
Accuracy
Recommendations
PositiveClass Estimated Actual Estimated tuneRanger ranger mtry min.node.size sample.fraction
1 501.3 111.877 86.260 86.64 86.56 3 12 0.383
0 485.1 105.110 86.315 86.46 86.50 4 6 0.232

The differences are negligible and vary between runs. I conclude there is no effective difference.

10.3 Positive Class, Factor Order

Here I make one more comparison - fitting and predicting with ranger against train_df and test_df as-is, with implicit factor ordering of 0, 1; and then again with explicit factor-ordering of 1,0.

which_class <- function(.train = train_df, .test = test_df) {
    fit  <- ranger(fc, .train)
    pred <- predict(fit, .test)
    cm   <- confusionMatrix(pred$predictions, factor(.test$disease_present))
    c(
        accuracy = 100*cm$overall[['Accuracy']],
        correct  = diag(cm$table) |> sort()
    )
}

zero_first <- which_class()
one_first  <- which_class(
    train_df |> mutate(disease_present = factor(disease_present, ordered=T, levels=c(1,0))),
    test_df  |> mutate(disease_present = factor(disease_present, ordered=T, levels=c(1,0)))
)
    
cbind(zero_first, one_first) |>
    kable(caption = 'Factor Order Effect?') |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = 'left')
Factor Order Effect?
zero_first one_first
accuracy 85.94 86.04
correct.1 740.00 743.00
correct.0 3557.00 3559.00

Additional evidence for the same conclusion - differences are minimal and variable.

10.4 RandomForest Decision Tree

I like to get a glimpse into the “thinking” of these models, and for that I look to a randomForest decision tree. Unfortunately there is a trade-off between depth of information and clarity. To help, I shorten the column names and hackishly round digits to two decimals.

fit <- randomForest(
    factor(disease_present) ~ .,
    train_df |> dplyr::rename(h2o = rainfall, tmp = temperature, pH = soil_ph, hum = humidity),
    ntree = 20
)
simplest_tree <- which.min(fit$forest$ndbigtree)
fit$forest$xbestsplit <- round(fit$forest$xbestsplit, 2)  # 'digits' workaround
plot.getTree(
    fit,
    k     = simplest_tree,
    depth = 6,
    main  = 'RandomForest Decision Tree'
)

10.5 RandomForest - Other Metrics

Here I look at metrics in addition to accuracy.

Prevalence was known from the class distribution, the 75% portion of the positive class (0, healthy).

Sensitivity, or true positive, is high; and Specificity, or true negative, is fairly low. It seems plausible that those numbers are reflective of the 75/25% distribution.

I am uncertain what to conclude. Accuracy and precision seem pretty good, but sensitivity and specificity are not well balanced.

metrics <- c('Prevalence', 'Sensitivity', 'Specificity', 'Precision', 'F1')
fit   <- randomForest(factor(disease_present) ~ ., train_df, ntree = 20)
pred  <- predict(fit, test_df)
cm    <- confusionMatrix(pred, factor(test_df$disease_present))
cm$byClass |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column() |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = rowname, values_from = `cm$byClass`) |>
    select(all_of(metrics)) |>
    mutate(
        Accuracy = cm$overall[['Accuracy']]*100,
        F_meas   = caret::F_meas(
            data      = factor(train_df$disease_present),
            reference = factor(test_df$disease_present)
        )
    ) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = 'Ranger Classification Metrics') |>
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = 'bordered', full_width = FALSE, position = 'left')
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy F_meas
0.754 0.94 0.585 0.874 0.906 85.28 0.775

11 Conclusions

Once again, I have not been able to improve models significantly beyond what I consider the baseline. It seems the models’ default modes are nearly ideal. But, as mentioned in the Introduction I’m gauging against others on Kaggle, and my best of 87% rivals what I’ve seen.

My primary goal was to continue learning, and here in particular I learned:

  • sink and nullfile, for something analogous to > /dev/null

    But - danger, danger - do not leave a lingering sink object!

  • curl_download, to pull down Kaggle data without API credentials

  • ellipsis (...) argument, used here to make my model framework smaller and more flexible

  • more kable, especially making narrow tables NOT full width, and left-aligned

  • labeller, for plotting meaningful words instead of 0,1

  • tuneRanger package and tools

  • datatable, which I used via Perl years ago

  • the effect, if any, of which class is positive

  • tryCatch, to make the framework more robust

This was my first major exposure to library conflicts. I believe the only instance I had seen prior was needing to fully qualify dplyr::select. Here, I also had to qualify ggcorrplot::cor_pmat and caret::train, neither of which was the least bit obvious; and later dplyr::rename and dplyr::mutate. I am beginning to think that fully-qualifying is a good practice.

This project turned up a few new interesting topics that I will revisit in upcoming projects.

  • Using tidymodels and associated packages to create tuning recipes and workflows, which seems to be an alternative to train
  • Using dtree, for what seems to provide a simple ensemble of decision-tree models
  • Perhaps function factories to reduce near-redundant code in my framework
